name: ps
summary: Snapshot of running processes with their IDs, owners, CPU and memory use.

install.note: Slim containers may lack ps entirely.

compat: procps ps accepts both BSD style (ps aux) and POSIX style (ps -ef). BusyBox ps ignores most options and prints a simple list; use ps -o to choose columns where supported.

examples.title: All processes, BSD style
examples.explain: a = all users, u = user-oriented columns, x = include processes without a terminal.
examples.output: USER owner, PID process ID, %CPU and %MEM usage, RSS resident memory in KiB, STAT state (R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible I/O wait, Z zombie), COMMAND command line.

examples.title: Top memory users
examples.explain: Sorts by memory descending (the - prefix) and keeps the header plus 9 processes.
options: Sort by memory use, highest first (procps)

examples.title: Chosen columns for one process
examples.explain: PPID is the parent process ID; ETIME how long it has been running.

name: top
summary: Live, continuously updated view of CPU, memory and the busiest processes.

install.note: htop is a friendlier alternative you can install separately.

compat: Interactive keys (procps top): P sort by CPU, M sort by memory, 1 show each CPU, q quit. BusyBox top has fewer keys.

examples.title: Open the live view
examples.explain: The header shows uptime, load average (1, 5, 15 minutes), CPU usage split into us (user), sy (kernel), wa (waiting for I/O), and memory. Press q to quit.

examples.title: One snapshot for a log or a bug report
examples.explain: -b batch mode prints plain text instead of drawing the screen; -n 1 takes a single sample.

name: kill
summary: Send a signal to a process, normally to ask it to stop.

install.note: Shell builtin; /bin/kill comes from procps or util-linux.

compat: You can only signal your own processes unless you are root. Find the PID with pgrep or ps first.

examples.title: List signal names
examples.explain: SIGTERM (15) asks politely; SIGINT (2) is what Ctrl+C sends; SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored.

examples.title: Ask a process to exit
examples.explain: Sends SIGTERM, giving the program a chance to save data and clean up. No output means the signal was delivered; 'No such process' means the PID is gone.
examples.warning: Stops the program; unsaved work in it is lost. Confirm the PID belongs to the right program (ps -p <pid> -o pid,cmd).
options: Process ID from ps or pgrep

examples.title: Force-kill a process that ignores SIGTERM
examples.explain: Last resort after kill <pid> had no effect for a few seconds. A process in state D (waiting on I/O or a driver) may not die even with -9 until the I/O completes.
examples.warning: SIGKILL gives the process no chance to clean up: temporary files, locks and partially written data may be left behind.

name: pgrep
summary: Find process IDs by name (pgrep), or signal them by name (pkill).
compat: The pattern is a regular expression matched against the process name (or full command line with -f), so short patterns can match more processes than you expect.

examples.title: Find processes by name with their command lines
examples.explain: Prints PID and full command line. Exit status 1 means no process matched.

examples.title: Your own processes only
examples.explain: Restricts matches to processes owned by you.

examples.title: Stop processes by name
examples.explain: -x requires the whole process name to match exactly. Run pgrep -a -x <name> first: pkill signals everything that pgrep would list.
examples.warning: Sends SIGTERM to EVERY matching process. Without -x, a pattern like 'sh' would also match bash, ssh and others.

name: jobs
summary: Run programs in the background and move them between foreground and background (jobs, fg, bg, &).

install.note: Shell builtins (job control must be enabled, which it is in interactive shells).

compat: Background jobs belong to your terminal; closing it usually stops them. Use nohup, tmux or screen for work that must survive logout.

examples.title: Start a command in the background
examples.explain: The shell prints a job number like [1] and the PID, then gives you the prompt back. Output still appears in the terminal; redirect it to a file to avoid clutter.

examples.title: List jobs, then bring one to the foreground
examples.explain: Shows job numbers, PIDs and states. Then fg %1 brings job 1 back; Ctrl+Z suspends the foreground job and bg resumes it in the background.

examples.title: Keep a command running after logout
examples.explain: nohup makes the command ignore the hang-up signal sent when the terminal closes. Both output streams go to <logfile>.
options: Send errors to the same file

name: lsof
summary: List open files: which process is using a file, device, or network port.
compat: Without root you only see your own processes. For ports, ss -ltnp is usually preinstalled and gives similar information.

examples.title: Who has this file or device open?
examples.explain: Explains 'Device or resource busy' when unmounting, or a serial port that will not open.

examples.title: Which process is using a TCP port?
examples.explain: Fixes 'Address already in use' by showing which program already holds the port.
examples.warning: Runs as root only so it can see other users' processes; it does not change anything.

examples.title: All files opened by one process
examples.explain: Shows libraries, log files, sockets and devices the process holds open.

name: watch
summary: Re-run a command every few seconds and show its output full-screen.
compat: -d (highlight differences) is procps only. Press Ctrl+C to exit.

examples.title: Watch memory every second
examples.explain: Re-runs free -h every second, handy while a program is running.

examples.title: Watch the newest kernel messages while plugging in a device
examples.explain: Put pipelines in quotes so watch runs the whole thing. -d highlights what changed between runs. dmesg may need sudo on some distributions.
